## From arrays to a GPU decision {#path}

. . .

:::{.nonincremental}
1. Choose the **device and precision** explicitly.
2. Separate **resident computation** from the **complete job**.
3. Compare workloads at the **required accuracy**. [π activity](#a6)
:::

. . .

[Script](../scripts/4_memory_and_gpu.jl) · [Julia notebook](../pluto/4_memory_and_gpu.jl) · [Python notebook](../python/4_memory_and_gpu_python.ipynb) · [No GPU](../gpu-fallback.qmd)

::: {.notes}
Session 3, minutes 95–145, including the 30-minute activity. This chapter combines dispatch,
measurement, batching and reduction. Use library operations; manual kernels are optional.
The decision concerns enough parallel work, reuse on the device, and full runtime at a
specified accuracy. Do not describe GPU threads as slower CPU cores or compare their counts directly.
:::

# Device, data and measurement {style="text-align: center;"}

## Same operation, another array type

. . .

```julia
A = rand(Float32, 3, 3); B = rand(Float32, 3, 3)
Ag = CuArray(A); Bg = CuArray(B)   # copy to GPU memory, same dtype
A * B                            # CPU
Ag * Bg                          # GPU method
```

. . .

> Dispatch selects an implementation from the argument types; the mathematical operation is unchanged.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "4. Device and precision". RAM and GPU memory are separate here.
CuArray(A) preserves A's element type; the convenience function cu may narrow Float64 to
Float32. Both copies and changes in precision must be stated. The GPU has many execution lanes,
but a CUDA thread is not comparable to a CPU core. Small workloads may not amortize overhead.
:::

## Specify accuracy before comparing

- Hold **input values and dtype** fixed for a deterministic comparison.
- Check the result against a **justified numerical tolerance**.
- For Monte-Carlo, also specify the **statistical accuracy target**.

. . .

> A faster Float32 calculation is useful only if its accuracy meets the requirement.

::: {.notes}
The default dtype can differ across libraries. FP32, FP64 and accelerator math modes may
change speed and error; do not call Float32 universally the GPU's native precision.
For π, the standard error is about 1.64/sqrt(n), as in module 1. This is not a guaranteed
absolute-error bound. CPU/GPU RNGs may produce different samples even at the same n.
:::

## Time completed work

. . .

```julia
CUDA.@sync Ag * Bg   # wait for the GPU operation before stopping the timer
```

Python equivalent for a resident calculation:

```python
torch.cuda.synchronize()
start = time.perf_counter()
Yg = Ag @ Bg
torch.cuda.synchronize()
seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
```

::: {.notes}
Warm up before repeated measurements. GPU operations can enqueue work and return before
it finishes; an unsynchronized host timer can measure submission rather than completion.
The first synchronization excludes earlier work; the second includes this product's completion.
Returning a result to the CPU can also synchronize, but state the timed scope explicitly.
:::

## What crosses the bus?

. . .

Historical observations on the course machine, **64 MiB per Float32 matrix**:

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Upload one matrix | 8.5 ms |
| Product, inputs resident | 35 ms |
| Download one matrix | 52 ms |

. . .

> A complete product needs **two uploads, the product, and its result download**.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "What the copy costs". Historical rounded minimum timings include allocation
for the transfer calls. Direction alone does not determine transfer cost; buffers, memory
allocation and runtime state matter. 2×8.5+35+52 ≈104 ms is a derived estimate, not an observed
complete-job time. Measure the complete path rather than summing independently timed minima.
:::

## Resident work and the complete job

. . .

```julia
# Inputs already on the GPU; result remains there
CUDA.@sync Ag * Bg

# Host inputs → upload → product → host result
matmul_to_host(A, B) = CUDA.@sync Array(CuArray(A) * CuArray(B))
```

. . .

> Keep intermediate data on the GPU when possible; return the **result the application requires**.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "The matrix product, resident and complete". Compare both scopes with CPU A*B
using identical Float32 inputs. Check the returned matrix, not only the runtime. The function
includes allocations, both uploads, the operation, synchronization and the download.
A matrix-valued application cannot replace its required result by a scalar merely to avoid transfer.
:::

# Parallel work and batching {style="text-align: center;"}

## Matrix size and GPU runtime

. . .

Predict the GPU speedup for **N = 64** and for **N = 4096**.

. . .

| N | CPU | Resident GPU | Observed speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 0.01 ms | 0.03 ms | 0.25× |
| 512 | 1.15 ms | 0.09 ms | 13.0× |
| 2048 | 69.8 ms | 3.02 ms | 23.1× |
| 4096 | hundreds of ms | ~35 ms | ~15–20× |

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "5. GPU workload size". Historical rounded observations from the course laptop,
Float32, inputs already resident, synchronized GPU computation; transfers excluded.
Ratios were computed before rounding the displayed times. These thresholds are not universal.
Launch/synchronization overhead matters for small work. The table alone does not establish
why throughput changes at the largest size; test power state, dimensions and library choices.
:::

## Batching on resident GPU data

. . .

Reference `W`: **4096² Float32**. Inputs remain on the device.

| B | ms / batch | µs / example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.41 | 410 |
| 8 | 0.42 | 52.5 |
| 64 | 0.45 | 7.0 |
| 256 | 2.23 | 8.7 |

. . .

> Larger batches can improve throughput; latency and buffer requirements still constrain the choice.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "Batching on the GPU". Historical rounded synchronized product times; data
generation/transfers are excluded. Per-example figures are derived from these rounded times.
Low throughput at B=1 does not measure utilization or imply that the CPU is necessarily faster.
The best batch is an empirical choice, as in module 4. The live code records its own resource budget.
:::

# Monte-Carlo π on the GPU {style="text-align: center;"}

## Generate, count and reduce on the device

. . .

```julia
function pi_gpu(n)
    x = CUDA.rand(Float32, n)
    y = CUDA.rand(Float32, n)
    inside = (x.^2 .+ y.^2) .<= 1f0
    return 4 * sum(inside) / n
end
```

- The points are generated **on the GPU**, without uploading point vectors.
- A library reduction returns **one scalar** to the host.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "6. Monte-Carlo π on the GPU". The complete estimator includes allocations,
random generation, comparison, reduction, synchronization and scalar return. The reduction
is parallel; its final stages expose less parallelism. This is the module-3 local-count pattern
implemented by library kernels. 1f0 is 1 represented as Float32.
:::

::: {.notes}
First check the same four fixed points on CPU and GPU, then interpret random π estimates using
SE ≈1.64/sqrt(n). Choose and state a statistical-accuracy target; a small-n speedup may be
irrelevant if that n is insufficient. Do not demand identical random estimates across devices.
The no-GPU route has the same reasoning objectives and does not invent device timings.
:::

## A speedup depends on its baseline {#a6-debrief}

. . .

Historical example: 100 million points, GPU Float32 estimator **~12 ms**.

| CPU implementation | Observed speedup |
|---|---|
| Float32 arrays, allocations included | ~35× |
| Scalar loop, Float64 draws | ~25× |

. . .

> Compare implementations at an acceptable accuracy; these ratios do **not isolate hardware alone**.

::: {.notes}
The RNGs, precision and allocation patterns differ. Ask which sizes meet the students' stated
accuracy target, what stays on the device, and what costs are timed. A failed acceleration or
missing GPU can still lead to a valid conditional decision with a proposed next measurement.
:::

## Three questions for the GPU decision {#decision}

. . .

:::{.nonincremental}
1. **Is there enough parallel work?**
2. **Can intermediate data stay on the GPU?**
3. **Is the complete job faster at the required accuracy?**
:::

# Optional — coalescing {#appendix style="text-align: center;"}

## Neighboring threads, neighboring addresses

- CUDA groups threads into **warps of 32**.
- Neighboring addresses can be served by **fewer memory transactions**.
- Scattered addresses can require more transactions.

. . .

> CPU locality concerns a thread's access sequence; coalescing also concerns addresses accessed by neighboring GPU threads.

::: {.notes}
This CUDA example concerns NVIDIA warps. Do not equate a warp with 32 CPU cores or assume
that all divergent threads progress in strict lockstep. Map thread indices to the actual layout.
:::

## Coalescing: a controlled permutation

. . .

```julia
idx = CuArray(Int32.(((0:N-1) .* s) .% N .+ 1))
a[idx]   # same elements in a different order when gcd(s,N) = 1
```

| Stride | Historical time |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2.24 ms |
| 33 | 5.40 ms |
| 1023 | 12.3 ms |

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "7. Optional — coalescing". N=20 million; require a permutation so this does
not merely reread a smaller subset. gcd(33,N)=gcd(1023,N)=1. This operation also reads the
index array and writes an output. Identify all arrays before assigning the ratio to one cause.
:::

## Test a memory-traffic explanation

. . .

Compute the index in the kernel rather than loading an index array:

```julia
i = (blockIdx().x - 1) * blockDim().x + threadIdx().x
j = ((i - 1) * s) % n + 1
out[i] = a[j]
```

Historical stride-33 / stride-1 ratios: **2.4×** with `a[idx]`, **4.18×** with computed indices.

. . .

> Index arithmetic and allocation also change: this comparison does not isolate one effect.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "Test that explanation". The output is still written contiguously. Nominally,
source reads are one third of the gather's bytes versus one half without an index array,
but nominal bytes are not memory-transaction counts. Validate the permutation's output too.
:::

## Eight answers in two seconds? {#a7-debrief}

. . .

**Hypothetical example:** B = 8, 32 generated tokens per answer, batch completed in 2 s.

. . .

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Total throughput | 128 generated tokens/s |
| Amortized time per answer | 0.25 s |
| Wait for each answer, returned together | 2 s |

. . .

> Where is the parallelism, if each token depends on the previous ones?

::: {.notes}
Discuss internal matrix operations and independent sequences; connect W*x to W*X and weight reuse.
Successive tokens remain dependent. More throughput need not reduce batch latency. Timings alone
identify neither utilization nor a particular bottleneck. Include memory and service waiting constraints.
The notebook fixes output length, includes prefill and decoding, excludes text conversion and transfers,
and compares successive requests with a single batch for equal total work. These numbers are fictitious.
:::
